title: Velocity graphs and components
vocab: Above zero adds displacement; below zero subtracts it.
Add area sizes, including the return trip.
A vector’s signed part along one axis.
Name the starting axis and turn direction.

example.prompt: A cart moves at +3 m/s for 2 s, then −1 m/s for 2 s. Find its displacement and total distance.
example.given:
v₁ = +3 m/s
v₂ = −1 m/s
2 s per interval
example.equation: Use areas because each interval has steady v.
example.remark: Return travel reduces Δx, not distance.

thread: For fictional XJ, the area of a velocity–time graph gives a change in position. Components separate motion toward Earth from motion across its line of sight.
target: I can read v–t areas and resolve velocity into components.

title: Position predictions and their limits
vocab: Position when the chosen interval begins.
An allowed range, not a standard deviation.
The ± value; full width is twice as large.
A condition treated as true, such as steady v.

example.prompt: A cart starts at 8 ± 0.5 m and moves at −2.0 ± 0.1 m/s for an exact 3 s. Find its predicted position interval.
example.given:
x₀ = 8 ± 0.5 m
v = −2.0 ± 0.1 m/s
t = 3 s; steady v
example.equation:
Steady v: x𝒻 = x₀ + vt.
Add input bounds.

thread: XJ's position and velocity readings have limits. A forecast should show both the central result and the interval allowed by those limits; the interval does not give an impact probability.
target: I can predict a position and state its uncertainty.

title: Add vectors by their components
vocab: Signed part along an axis; keep axes fixed.
Sum: first tail to final tip.
Both component signs locate the direction.

example.prompt: Two displacements are A = (6, −4) m and B = (−4, 8) m. Find their sum's magnitude and direction.
example.given:
+x is east
+y is north
A and B use these axes.
example.equation:
Add x and y.
Use the right triangle.

thread: XJ's motion must be tracked in more than one direction. Adding signed components keeps sideways motion in the forecast instead of treating every displacement as motion toward Earth.
target: I can add vectors and resolve their signed components.

title: Acceleration, signs and turning around
vocab: Change in velocity divided by elapsed time.
v and a have the same direction in 1D.
v and a oppose each other before the turn.
v = 0 for an instant; a can be nonzero.

example.prompt: A cart's velocity changes uniformly from +6 m/s to −2 m/s in 4 s. Find its acceleration and the time it reverses.
example.remark: Slows for 3 s, then speeds up to the left.

thread: A change in XJ's velocity requires an acceleration term in the forecast. Its sign alone does not show whether the asteroid is speeding up; compare the directions of velocity and acceleration.
target: I can find acceleration from changes in velocity.

title: Choose an equation for steady acceleration
vocab: Equal velocity changes in equal times.
Signed change in position, not distance.
Test with units, a graph or another equation.

example.prompt: A car moving at +20 m/s brakes at −4 m/s² until it stops. Find its stopping distance, then check the result.
example.remark: 5 s to stop; area also gives 50 m.

thread: For XJ, choose a relationship that fits both the known values and the motion being assumed. A graph provides a second check before a forecast is reported.
target: I can choose an equation for constant acceleration.

title: Balanced forces can mean steady motion
vocab: An unforced object keeps its velocity.
Vector sum of external forces on a system.
More mass resists velocity change more.
Net force zero; v constant, not always zero.

example.prompt: A cart is at −2 m, moving at +3 m/s. Its external forces balance for the next 4 s. Find its final position.
example.equation:
First law: constant v.
x𝒻 = x₀ + vt.

thread: XJ needs no forward force simply to keep moving. Gravity can still change its velocity, so treating a short interval as steady motion is an approximation to be tested.
target: I can explain steady motion with Newton’s first law.

title: Name each force and its source
vocab: Rope’s pull along itself, away from the object.
The object a force acts on; also name its source.

example.prompt: A 3 kg crate rests on a table. A vertical rope pulls up with 10 N. Find the table's normal force. Use g = 9.8 N/kg.

thread: A forecast of XJ's changing motion needs real interactions, not a made-up motion force. Name the attracting body for each gravitational force before adding the forces.
target: I can name each force, its source and its receiver.

title: Change mass while net force stays fixed
vocab: All moving mass, including any hanger.
A value held fixed for a fair comparison.
Double M halves a at fixed net force.
Plot a against 1/M to get an ideal line.

example.prompt: Under the same net force, a 1 kg system accelerates at 4 m/s² and a 2 kg system at 2 m/s². Predict a for a 3 kg system.
example.given:
M₁ = 1 kg; a₁ = 4 m/s²
M₂ = 2 kg; a₂ = 2 m/s²
same net force

thread: For the same force, a more massive XJ changes velocity less quickly. The comparison needs the same net force; a larger gravitational force can change that result.
target: I can test how mass affects acceleration at fixed force.

title: Change force while total mass stays fixed
vocab: The pull before resistance is subtracted.
Fixed friction shifts the driving-force line down.

example.prompt: A 2 kg system slides with 0.4 N of opposing friction. Compare acceleration with driving forces of 2 N and 4 N.
example.given:
M = 2 kg
f = 0.4 N
Fdrive = 2 N, then 4 N
example.remark: Driving force doubles; a does not.

thread: A proposed push on XJ must be added to every other external force. Only the net force belongs in the calculation of acceleration.
target: I can test F = ma while keeping total mass fixed.

title: Net force first, then interpret the motion
vocab: Add signed forces along the same axis.
Velocity change from net force per mass.
Current motion; it can oppose a.
Opposite v and a: slows before reversal.

example.prompt: A 4 kg cart has forces of 12 N right and 4 N left. Its initial velocity is −3 m/s. Find a and v after 1 s.
example.given:
m = 4 kg
Fright = 12 N; Fleft = 4 N
vᵢ = −3 m/s
example.equation:
Sum forces first.
ΣFₓ = maₓ.
v = vᵢ + aₓt.
example.remark: Still leftward; speed is now 1 m/s.

thread: The direction of XJ's net force tells us its acceleration direction. Its existing velocity must also be known to say whether it speeds up, slows down or turns.

title: Equal forces, different accelerations
target: I can identify force pairs acting on different objects.
vocab: A-on-B and B-on-A: equal and opposite.
Two objects; use separate force diagrams.
Same force size: smaller mass, larger a.
Pair forces cancel internally for combined A+B.

example.prompt: Cart A has mass 1 kg; cart B has mass 3 kg. Their interaction pushes A left and B right with 6 N each. Find both accelerations.
example.equation:
F = ma on each cart.
No other horizontal forces.
example.remark: A has 3 times B’s acceleration size.

thread: Earth and fictional XJ pull on each other equally at the same instant. Their very different masses give different accelerations; the pair does not cancel in XJ's own force diagram.

title: Draw forces on one chosen object
vocab: The receiver of every force in the diagram.
A force from outside the chosen boundary.
Use one scale to show each force’s size.
Sum of forces, not another interaction.

example.prompt: A rope lifts a 2 kg lamp with upward acceleration 1.5 m/s². Find the tension. Use g = 9.8 m/s².
example.remark: T and W are not a third-law pair.

thread: An XJ force diagram contains forces on XJ, not the forces XJ exerts on other bodies. Defining that boundary keeps the acceleration calculation consistent.
target: I can draw every force on one object, with arrows to scale.

title: Choose useful axes on an incline
vocab: Along the ramp; choose downhill as +.
Straight out of the ramp, usually not vertical.
mg sin θ along; mg cos θ into the ramp.
No motion through the surface: a⊥ = 0.

example.prompt: A 2 kg block slides down a 30° ramp with 2 N friction uphill. Find its acceleration and normal force. Use g = 9.8 m/s².
example.equation:
mg sin θ − f = ma∥
N = mg cos θ

thread: A suitable set of axes can simplify the forces changing XJ's path. Components are calculation tools; they must not be counted again as extra forces.
target: I can use a force diagram to find acceleration on a ramp.

title: Static and kinetic friction
vocab: Adjusts to prevent slip, up to a limit.
fₛ,max = μₛN; fₛ can be smaller.
Find the perpendicular force balance first.

example.prompt: For this box, compare a 6 N pull while at rest with a 10 N pull after sliding starts. Use g = 9.8 m/s²; pulls are horizontal.
example.equation:
Check μₛN.
Sliding: use μₖN, then net force.

thread: Surface friction is not a force that continually brakes XJ in empty space. Gravitational forces can still change its velocity, and atmospheric drag would matter in an atmosphere.

title: Equilibrium balances components
vocab: Zero a: forces sum to zero on each axis.
Equal angles and loading: equal tensions.
v = 0 alone does not prove balance.

example.prompt: A 40 N sign hangs at rest from two equal ropes, each 30° above horizontal. Find the tension in each rope.

thread: Zero net force would give XJ a constant velocity, not a guaranteed stop. Analysts must check each coordinate direction before treating its motion as steady.

title: Find the first wrong step and repair it
vocab: Name what is found: position, speed, etc.
Direction uses signs; speed is a size.
Sum all forces on the same object.
Use a graph or another equation.

example.prompt: A 3 kg cart has 9 N right and 3 N left. Someone writes a = 9/3 = 3 m/s². Explain and repair the first wrong step.
example.given:
m = 3 kg
right is +
forces: +9 N and −3 N
example.equation: Use net force, not the largest force.

thread: Before the fictional XJ forecast is shared, check its signs, units, starting coordinates and force sums. Repairing the first wrong step can change every later result.

title: Connect forces to velocity and position
vocab: Net force → a → velocity and position.
Keep one start and end time throughout.
v can cross zero while a keeps its sign.
Add positive and negative pieces of Δx.

example.prompt: A 2 kg cart starts at 1 m with velocity −2 m/s. A constant +4 N net force acts for 3 s. Find final velocity and position.
example.given:
m = 2 kg; ΣF = +4 N
x₀ = 1 m; vᵢ = −2 m/s
t = 3 s
example.equation:
Find a from force.
Then steady-a equations.

thread: XJ’s forecast needs its present motion and the forces changing it. Use one reference frame through the entire calculation.

title: Plan a prediction in two dimensions
vocab: Keep the origin and axes fixed.
Signed x and y parts; calculate separately.
Make all units match before substituting.
State assumptions, such as steady velocity.

example.prompt: A probe starts at (−20, 5) m and moves at 10 m/s, 30° from +x toward +y, for 2 s. Find its new coordinates.
example.given:
x₀ = −20 m; y₀ = 5 m
v = 10 m/s; θ = 30°
t = 2 s; steady v

thread: For fictional XJ, name the frame, units and motion assumptions. Fixed Earth and steady velocity are classroom simplifications.
target: I can plan a prediction using evidence and fixed axes.

title: Defend and revise a forecast
vocab: Result, units, time, direction and range.
A measurement or calculation supporting a step.
An uncertain input or missing effect.
Name the change and show its effect.

example.prompt: Keep x₀ = 8 ± 0.5 m and exact t = 3 s. A new measurement changes v from −2.0 to −1.5 ± 0.1 m/s. Update the forecast.

thread: Show the evidence behind XJ’s forecast and what changed after review. Separate the physics from cost and feasibility decisions.
target: I can defend a prediction, state limits and revise it.
